name: request-reply
intent: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
context: Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
benefits: Turns one-way messaging into a two-way conversation: the caller gets a result or a domain error instead of fire-and-forget, without inventing an ad-hoc protocol per call.

Correlation - an identifier or a private reply channel - lets many requests share one reply channel and lets each arriving reply be dispatched to the right waiter, which is what makes concurrent in-flight calls possible.
An explicit timeout and cancellation rule bounds waiting: a missing reply becomes a defined error or fallback instead of a hung thread and an unbounded set of pending entries.
The caller's task is freed (asynchronous callback variant) or cheaply blocked (structured-concurrency variant), so throughput is no longer tied to the number of outstanding calls.
Reply correlation is transport-independent: the same shape works over HTTP, gRPC, a broker queue, a WebSocket or an in-process channel.
Late or orphaned replies have a defined fate (dropped, logged or dead-lettered), which keeps state bounded under failure and restart.
tradeoffs: Time coupling: the caller now depends on the replier's availability and latency, so a slow or dead replier converts directly into deadline violations unless degradation is designed in.
Pending state must be managed: correlation entries, timers and cancellation registrations leak if a reply is lost, duplicated or arrives after the timeout - the pattern's dominant failure mode.

Round trips cost latency and capacity: a synchronous block binds a thread per outstanding call, while the asynchronous variants move the cost into bookkeeping and context propagation (correlation ids, reply addresses, deadlines across hops).
The reply path is a new inbound surface: a forged or replayed reply can satisfy a pending request unless correlation ids are unguessable and replies are authenticated.
Partial failure is inherent: the caller can time out while the replier has already performed the work, so correctness depends on idempotent operations rather than on the timeout alone.
Duplicate and out-of-order replies are undefined unless the protocol adds ordering or deduplication rules; implementations must decide whether a second reply is ignored or an error.

participants.responsibility: Formulates the request, publishes it on the request channel with a reply address or correlation token, and consumes exactly one reply per request.
Consumes the request, performs the operation and returns exactly one reply to the address named by the request, echoing the correlation identifier.
Point-to-point channel (occasionally publish-subscribe) that carries requests from requestor to replier: a broker queue, an RPC method, a socket or an in-process mailbox.
Destination of the reply - a private or anonymous queue, a reply-to address, a callback continuation or an in-process port. Almost always point-to-point, since replies must reach only the requestor.
Token that matches a reply to its request when several exchanges share a channel: a request id echoed by the replier, a private reply channel, or a runtime continuation handle.
Requestor-side component holding the pending requests; routes each arriving reply to exactly one waiter (future completion, callback, channel send) and triggers timeout and cancellation handling.

use_cases: Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.
avoid_when: Information flows one way only (events, telemetry, notifications): use Event Message with publish-subscribe and no reply path.
Throughput matters more than per-request confirmation: batch or stream results instead of paying one round trip per unit.
The receiver cannot answer (fire-and-forget commands): use Command Message with a separate outcome channel or an asynchronous completion token.
A local call would do: request-reply over a broker for something a direct method call or shared memory could serve adds latency, failure modes and operational cost.
Reply latency can exceed the caller's budget and no fallback exists: prefer an asynchronous callback plus a state query over a blocking wait.
The exchange is really a conversation (several messages with shared state): use Message Sequence or a process manager instead of one request and one reply.
anti_patterns: Blocking receive with no timeout: one lost reply parks a thread or task forever and pending state grows without bound.
One reply queue shared by concurrent requests without a correlation identifier: whichever waiter reads first gets somebody else's reply (cross-talk).
Correlating on message content or ordering instead of a token: retries and reordering silently mis-associate replies.
A timeout that abandons the waiter but leaves the request running and the entry in the correlation table - leaks now, duplicated work later.
Chatty RPC between services: dozens of blocking round trips per operation, turning latency and partial failure into user-visible timeouts.
Trusting any reply that arrives on the reply channel: a forged or replayed reply satisfies a pending request unless the token is unguessable and the reply authenticated.
design_principles: Explicit correlation: never rely on arrival order or payload content to identify a reply.
Bounded waiting: every request carries a deadline, and the wait ends at the deadline, not when the replier decides to answer.
Exactly zero or one accepted reply per request: duplicates and late replies are defined as no-reply.
Fail fast and degrade explicitly: a missing reply is a first-class outcome (domain error, fallback, retry policy), not an exception to swallow.
Return address discipline: the replier answers on the address named by the request, not on a channel it chooses.
Resource ownership: pending entries, timers and listeners belong to the requestor and are released on reply, timeout or cancellation.
best_practices: Generate an unguessable unique correlation id per request, echo it unchanged in the reply, and validate it before completing a waiter.
Set the deadline at the caller and propagate it with the request, so every downstream hop shares one budget instead of adding its own.
On timeout or cancellation, remove pending state atomically and mark the request abandoned; make the operation idempotent so a late reply or retry cannot double-apply effects.
Prefer a private reply channel per requester (temporary queue, direct reply-to, inbox subject, continuation) where the transport supports it, and fall back to correlation ids where it does not.
Bound the number of in-flight requests and the size of the correlation table; shed load instead of queueing it indefinitely.
Record correlation ids and deadline outcomes on both sides: a request-reply interaction is only diagnosable when both halves log the same token.
Test the missing-reply path with a controllable clock or a fake replier; timeouts, duplicates and late replies are the cases that break in production.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Request-Reply (Message Construction chapter); the pattern's originating catalog (eip).
